reading.rtitle: The Team That Drew Its Own Close on a Wall
paras: Nine days. That was how long the monthly close took at the Warsaw service center when Marta Kowalska took it over, and nobody in the building thought that was strange. The team was not slow, and nobody was doing anything wrong. They were simply doing every step in an order that had never been decided by anyone — and in nine years, nobody had drawn that order on a wall.

So that is what she did first. She wrote the nine days on a whiteboard, step by step, and asked one question about each one: what has to be finished before this can start? The answers were almost always the same. Nothing could be reconciled until the last journal entry had been posted. Nothing could be posted until the cut-off had passed. Once the order was on the wall, in front of everybody, the problem stopped being an opinion and became a picture.

Then she moved two things, and only two. The first was the cut-off. Instead of midnight on the last calendar day, it now falls at six in the evening, which gives the team a full morning before anything else begins. The second was the accrual review. It used to happen at the very end, after everything else, when everybody had already been working for four days. As soon as she moved it to day two, the number of items the team had to flag for the controller dropped by half. By the time the fifth day arrives now, there is usually nothing left to argue about.

What did not change is the last hour. A variance report still goes to the controller before the sign-off, and Marta still reads every line of it out loud on a call. “People think a close is finished when the system says it is finished,” she says. “A close is finished when somebody has explained it, in one sentence, to a person who was not in the room.” Nine days became five. The last five minutes are still the ones she protects.

listenings.text: Hi, it is me. I am recording this instead of writing it, because it is long and you will read it faster than you can hear it, and I want you to hear it. Three things about next month's close. First, the cut-off moves. It is six in the evening on the last calendar day now, not midnight, and that is not a suggestion. Second, the accrual review happens on day two, not on day five. I know we have always done it at the end. That is exactly why we are moving it. And third, please do not wait until the variance report is finished before you flag something to me. If a number looks wrong on day one, tell me on day one. By the time the report is on my desk, it is already too late to be useful.

People always ask me which step of the close is the most expensive one, and they are always surprised by the answer. It is not the reconciliation. It is the ten minutes at the end, when somebody has to explain a number to a person who was not in the room while the work was done. I have seen a close finish on time, on the fifth working day, exactly as planned, and then lose three days in review, because the person who prepared it could not say, in one sentence, why the number moved. So here is what I tell my teams. Do the work in the right order, yes. But before you press send, write one sentence. What changed, and why. If you cannot write that sentence, the close is not finished. It is just posted.
